title: Indirect immunofluorescence
objective: Explain why indirect IF uses a primary and a labeled secondary antibody.

steps.title: Two antibodies, one signal
steps.body: In indirect **[[immunofluorescence|IF]]**, an unlabeled **[[primary antibody]]** binds the target. Then a fluorescent **[[secondary antibody]]** binds the primary. The secondary is raised against the primary's *species* (e.g. anti-rabbit), so one labeled secondary works for any rabbit primary.

steps.prompt: Order the steps of indirect IF.
steps.explanation: Block before primary to cut background; wash between layers to remove unbound antibody; DAPI marks nuclei at the end.

steps.prompt: Why use a labeled *secondary* instead of just labeling the primary?
options: Signal amplification: several secondaries bind one primary
It makes the overall staining protocol shorter and simpler
Secondaries are inherently more specific than primaries are
It removes the need for any washing steps in the protocol
steps.explanation: Several labeled secondaries can decorate one primary, amplifying signal — and one secondary serves many primaries of the same species.

variants.setup: You compare directly-labeled primary vs primary + labeled secondary.
variants.reveal: Multiple secondaries per primary amplify the signal, so indirect IF is usually brighter.

steps.scenario: You stain for two rabbit primaries at once, using one anti-rabbit secondary.
options: The secondary can't tell the two rabbit primaries apart
The two primaries will compete for each other's epitopes
The first primary will use up all of the secondary
steps.explanation: One anti-rabbit secondary binds both rabbit primaries, so you can't separate the two targets. Use primaries from different species with species-matched secondaries.
steps.followUp: Fix: pick primaries raised in different hosts (e.g. rabbit + mouse + goat) and matching secondaries.

variants.prompt: To stain two targets at once, your two primaries should be…
options: From different host species, with matched secondaries
From the same host species, at different dilutions
From any species, as long as both are monoclonal
variants.explanation: Different host species let species-specific secondaries separate the channels.
